item.text: {"text":"HSTU’s foundational [2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152) establishes a sequential-transduction architecture for nonstationary recommendation; its accuracy results do not establish whether a particular trained checkpoint uses recent intent, order, or broad historical associations. [Measuring Recency Bias (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) directly motivates distinguishing useful recency sensitivity from excessive dependence on recent items, reporting improved performance after mitigating measured recency bias. [Temporal-Aware and Intent Contrastive Learning (2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-8994/17/10/1634) also warns that random cropping, masking, and reordering can disrupt sequential semantics. Perturbation effects therefore require careful controls.\n\nA proposed diagnostic synthesis: freeze each category’s single HSTU checkpoint and compare identical users, targets, and candidate sets under original histories, equal-count recent versus oldest-item removal, and repeated order shuffles. Include shuffles that preserve the final item to separate earlier-order sensitivity from changes to the readout item. Remove padding before interventions, restore left padding afterward, and read the final nonpadding position. Measure paired target-rank change, reciprocal-rank change, and HR@10 flips; report per-category results and macro averages with user-level paired bootstrap intervals, retaining repeated perturbations within each user. Greater damage from recent removal suggests recency reliance; sensitivity to fixed-item-set shuffling suggests order dependence; resistance to shuffling alongside deletion sensitivity is consistent with broad historical associations. These are proposed sensitivity interpretations, not established HSTU findings or causal proof. Popularity-stratified results can help investigate shortcuts, but neither rank changes nor attention weights alone establish shortcut learning."}
